evidence.source: Zhengzhou University Center for Chinese Character Civilization, Chen Anqi
evidence.text: The study describes 北 from Shang oracle writing through the Shuowen seal form as two people turned back-to-back, with changes in stroke execution rather than a change in the proposed graphic conception. It cites oracle-bone examples 合集6057 and 29401, Shang bronze 集成2710, Western Zhou bronzes 集成2804 and 2819, Chu slips, and Qin slips. The author infers an original sense related to turning against or violating from this graphic conception, while acknowledging that secure excavated examples of that sense are lacking.
evidence.title: “北”字职用演变研究（一）

evidence.source: Zhengzhou University Center for Chinese Character Civilization, Chen Anqi
evidence.text: The study reports 北 used as a loan graph for ‘north’ from the Shang period, and says this became its principal and continuing function. It distinguishes this borrowing from the hypothesized back/turning-against sense and its proposed extensions. Its examples support Qin–Han written uses of 北 for ‘back’ and ‘back side’; betrayal, abandonment, and defeat uses are discussed from excavated and transmitted texts. These are the author's lexical and semantic analyses; they do not prove that the proposed written-attestation sequence is the chronology of spoken senses.
evidence.title: “北”字职用演变研究（一）

evidence.source: Zhengzhou University Center for Chinese Character Civilization, Chen Anqi
evidence.text: The study says 背, formed with 肉 as semantic element and 北 as phonetic, appears around the Qin–Han transition; it cites an early Western Han Zhangjiashan manuscript where 北 remains more common for the ‘back’ word. By the Eastern Han, a Wuwei medical manuscript and the Shuowen entry for 背 (‘spine/back’) support 背 as the usual graph. This concerns differentiation of written graphs, not the beginning of the spoken word.
evidence.title: “北”字职用演变研究（一）

evidence.source: Xu Shen, Shuowen Jiezi, text hosted by Wikisource
evidence.text: The Han dictionary states 北：𦮃也。從二人相背。凡北之屬皆從北: it glosses the word as 𦮃 and analyzes the graph as two people back-to-back. This records a Han-period lexicographic account; it does not independently establish the graph's earliest use or prove the proposed earlier sense.
evidence.title: 說文解字/08

evidence.text: The Guangyun record gives 北 fanqie 博墨切 and classifies it as a labial initial, first division, 德 rhyme, entering tone; its displayed reconstructions include pək and Baxter's Middle Chinese pok. This is medieval rhyme-dictionary evidence, not direct evidence for a Shang pronunciation.
evidence.title: 北 - 小韻 - 廣韻 - 韻典網

evidence.source: Wiktionary Chinese entry compiling historical phonology data
evidence.text: The page lists Mandarin běi and Cantonese Jyutping bak1, alongside distinct Old Chinese reconstructions Zhengzhang *pɯːɡ (2003) and Baxter–Sagart *pˤək (2014 system 1.1). These reconstructions are framework-specific and should not be combined as if they were a single pronunciation.
evidence.title: 北 - 维基词典，自由的多语言词典

evidence.text: The entry analyzes 背 as a phonosemantic graph with 北 as phonetic and 月 ‘flesh’ as semantic. It reports Zhengzhang values 北 *pɯːɡ and 背 *pɯːɡs / *bɯːɡs, and Baxter–Sagart 背 values /*m-pˤək-s/ for ‘turn one's back on’ and /*pˤək-s/ for ‘the back’. The comparison supports a phonetic relationship within these reconstruction systems, with derivational differences in 背; 北 is not itself a phonetic component in its own graph.
evidence.title: 背 - Wiktionary, the free dictionary

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Republic of Korea, Basic Korean Dictionary
evidence.text: The official dictionary associates 北 with Korean 북 (buk) for the northern direction. This documents a modern reading and meaning only.
evidence.title: 한국어기초사전: 북

evidence.text: The page gives 北 with kana きた and romanization kita for ‘north.’ It documents a modern Japanese lexical reading, not a Japanese origin for the character or word.
evidence.title: 北 kita (north) - Japanese Dictionary

evidence.text: The file page describes 北-oracle.svg as a modern vector depiction of the character in Shang oracle script style, not a photograph or scan of an inscribed artifact. It identifies source leads including Sinica Database and Chinese Etymology, and attributes the particular picture to image J19580 on hanziyuan.net. Reuse information points to the Richard Sears agreement; the Commons file describes the ancient glyph representation as public domain.
evidence.title: File:北-oracle.svg

evidence.text: The file page describes 北-bronze.svg as a vector depiction in bronze-script style. A third-party mirror entry surfaced in search but the Commons description page could not be opened during this research, so precise source and license provenance for this file was not confirmed. It is a modern redraw, not an ancient artifact photograph.
evidence.title: File:北-bronze.svg

evidence.text: The page describes 北-seal.svg as a modern SVG depiction of the Shuowen seal-script form and gives a source lead to the Sinica database and Chinese Etymology, specifically image S05949 in hanziyuan.net. Its licensing section states the SVG rendering of the ancient script is public domain, while the description also refers to a Richard Sears agreement. This is a modern redraw, not an artifact photograph.

gaps: The hypothesized original ‘turn against/back’ lexical sense is not securely attested by the excavated examples surveyed in the university study; the study calls the available excavated candidates uncertain. The Shang-period north loan is reported by that study, but I did not independently inspect a full oracle inscription context for a named earliest occurrence.

The etymological relation between the back-related word and ‘north’ remains a scholarly semantic proposal. No independently recoverable source-word name or object pronunciation is established or needed for this graph-borrowing account; similarity of reconstructed readings alone would not prove a borrowing event.

There is no sound component within 北. 北 is analyzed graphically as two back-to-back human figures; the northern-direction word is a whole-graph loan. For 背, 北 is a phonetic component, supported by cited reconstruction comparisons; this does not make 北 a phonetic component in its own formation.

The source study's chains from turning against to bodily back, back side, concealment, betrayal, abandonment and defeat vary in evidential strength. Some attestation dates concern written graphs, and cannot independently date each spoken sense or establish every semantic bridge.

The inspected sources do not provide a detailed, independently validated sequence of every intermediate graphic shape. The university author characterizes the conception as stable from Shang to seal form; the Commons images are modern redrawings, not artifact images.

The Commons bronze SVG description page returned a cache miss. Its direct image candidate is withheld because its file-specific reuse terms were not confirmed. The oracle SVG's description does not itself fully clarify the scope of the referenced Richard Sears agreement; reuse conditions should be checked against that agreement before deployment.
No image pixels were inspected in this research stage. Proposed glyphs are description-page candidates only.

items.period: Shang period, broadly c. 1300–1046 BCE in the Commons project classification
items.tradition: Shang oracle script style; modern vector redraw based on a referenced J19580 image, not an ancient artifact photograph
items.caption: A modern vector redraw of 北 in Shang oracle script style. The associated paleographic study cites oracle-bone examples for 北 and describes the two turned-away figures as the proposed graphic conception.
items.alt: Modern drawn oracle-script form of 北, shown as an early style candidate for comparison with later forms.
items.selection_reason: Provides an early graphic stage corresponding to inscription examples cited in the scholarly account and visually motivates the back-to-back interpretation. The linked paleographic context supports candidate identity; pixels remain for downstream inspection.
items.rights: Commons file page cites the Richard Sears website agreement and identifies the ancient-script SVG representation as public domain. Confirm the agreement's terms for this specific sourced redraw before reuse.

items.period: Shuowen Jiezi seal-form tradition, compiled in the Eastern Han (c. 100 CE); the file is a modern redraw of the dictionary style
items.tradition: Shuowen seal script style, not an excavated seal artifact
items.caption: A modern redraw of the 北 form presented in Shuowen seal-script style. Xu Shen's entry analyzes the character as two people back-to-back; this later dictionary form can be compared with the Shang-style candidate.
items.alt: Modern vector rendering of 北 in a Shuowen seal-script style.
items.selection_reason: Pairs a documented later dictionary-style rendering with the early oracle-style candidate to illustrate continuity claimed by the paleographic study without implying that the image is an artifact.
items.rights: Commons licensing states the SVG representation is public domain; the file description also references the Richard Sears agreement.

limitations.text: Both proposed images are modern digital redrawings of historical script styles, not photographs or scans of ancient inscriptions. No pixel inspection occurred at the research stage.
The bronze-style file was not included because the Commons description page could not be opened to verify identity and reuse terms.
